statements.quote: This chapter is an attempt of a treatment of *meaningful language spaces*.

It begins from the idea that the objects of study are not tokens, not words, and not even sentences, but the structured *possibility spaces* in which those things live — the space of all potential utterances, the space of all interpretations those utterances can generate, and the spaces of worlds, actions, and consequences in which those interpretations can be tested.
The guiding intuition is that meaning is not a substance carried by individual symbols.
Meaning is a property of structure: of the shape of the space, the geometry of its clusters and voids, and the maps that relate one space to another.
A single sentence, viewed in isolation, is almost meaningless.
What makes it meaningful is its position within a landscape — the nearby utterances, the distant ones, the gaps, the bridges, and the patterns that persist across scale.
The aim of this chapter is to make that intuition precise.

We will introduce a space of linguistic forms $X$, a space of semantic structures $S$, and an interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$; we will describe the geometric and topological features of these spaces; we will see how metaphor, ambiguity, and learning correspond to concrete geometric operations; and we will close with a set of open problems that frame a research programme.
This is not a finished theory.
It is a scaffold: a set of definitions, conjectures, and diagrams that make the central claims checkable, falsifiable, and extensible.
The most common modern approach to language treats it as a *statistical* object.

statements.quote: - **The gap grows linearly.** For a semantic manifold of intrinsic dimension $k$, the *normalized* expressibility gap $\eta(\varepsilon)$ — the fraction of semantic space lying within $\varepsilon$ of a boundary — satisfies $\eta(\varepsilon) = c\,\varepsilon + O(\varepsilon^{2})$ for small $\varepsilon$, a consequence of the coarea formula.

statements.quote: The coefficient $c$ is the total area of the Voronoi boundary, divided by how sharply the token scores rise away from it.

statements.quote: Measured across six transformer models (GPT-2, OPT, Pythia; 124M–1.5B parameters), the log-log slope of $\eta$ against $\varepsilon$ lands at **0.87–1.12** with $R^{2} > 0.985$ — a near-unit slope is exactly the linear law, confirmed.

statements.quote: \citeauthor{gardenfors2000conceptual} (\citeyear{gardenfors2000conceptual}) argued that the mind represents meaning as **geometry in quality spaces** — spaces built out of the dimensions by which we actually compare things: colour, temperature, height, weight, time, pitch.

statements.quote: In such a space an object is a *point*, a property is a *region*, and **similarity is distance**.

statements.quote: Gärdenfors also sorts cognition into three levels of resolution, and the sort is worth keeping in view because it is the cognitive-science twin of the token/meaning contrast this chapter opens on.

statements.quote: At the **subconceptual** level a route through a jungle is a stream of motor interactions, as fine-grained as firing patterns.

statements.quote: At the **conceptual** level the same route is a geometric path — "thirty metres west, then along the trail" — an abstraction that keeps the shape and drops the steps.

statements.quote: At the **symbolic** level it is a map, "A to B to C," where only names and their relations remain.
statements.section: Conceptual spaces: the geometry of thought

statements.quote: Meaning, on this view, lives at the conceptual level: the geometric one.
statements.section: Conceptual spaces: the geometry of thought

statements.quote: The token is a symbolic label pointing at a region of a conceptual space; the hidden state is a point wandering that space.
statements.section: Conceptual spaces: the geometry of thought

statements.quote: Colour is the canonical example, and it is a space of three **integral** dimensions: hue (a circle), saturation, and lightness.
statements.section: Conceptual spaces: the geometry of thought

statements.quote: You cannot specify a colour without fixing all three, which is what makes the dimensions *integral* rather than *separable* (you can, by contrast, judge an object's size while ignoring its colour).

statements.quote: Concrete spaces like this are why the abstract $S$ of the previous sections is not empty talk: meaning is not a bag of symbols, it is a landscape you can move through.

statements.quote: Convexity singles out the inductively respectable properties — a clean, falsifiable reason why the concepts we actually have are the ones we have.

statements.quote: And convexity is where the Voronoi thread pays off.

statements.quote: This is the logic of **coarse-graining** and, ultimately, the **renormalization group (RG)**:
statements.section: The renormalization-group view: meaning has no preferred scale

statements.quote: - **Coarse-graining.** At each scale, group the fine-grained degrees of freedom into effective variables.

statements.quote: The fine details that do not affect the large-scale structure are "integrated out," and what remains is the effective description seen at that scale.
statements.section: The renormalization-group view: meaning has no preferred scale

statements.quote: - **Scale invariance.** If the effective description looks the same at all scales (up to a rescaling), the system is *scale-free* — the RG notion of self-similarity.
statements.section: The renormalization-group view: meaning has no preferred scale

statements.quote: - **Emergence.** New collective variables appear at each scale that do not exist at finer scales.
statements.section: The renormalization-group view: meaning has no preferred scale

statements.quote: These emergent variables are the "meanings" at that scale.
statements.section: The renormalization-group view: meaning has no preferred scale

statements.quote: - **Fixed points.** A scale-free system is described by an RG *fixed point*: a description that does not change under coarse-graining.

statements.quote: The distance from the fixed point controls how strongly the system depends on scale.
statements.section: The renormalization-group view: meaning has no preferred scale

statements.quote: - **Meaning is the image of form under $\pi$.** A form $x$ is meaningful to the extent that $\pi(x)$ is a well-defined, structured element of $S$.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: - **Ambiguity is the failure of $\pi$ to be a function.** When a single form $x$ can be interpreted in multiple ways, $\pi$ is not single-valued at $x$; it is a *multivalued* map, or a *relation*.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: Ambiguity is the branching of $\pi$.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: - **Understanding is the construction of $\pi$.** To understand a language is, in this view, to have built a usable approximation to the map $\pi$.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: Learning a language is learning a map from forms to meanings.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: - **Communication is the agreement of two $\pi$'s.** Speaker and listener each have their own interpretation map.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: Communication succeeds to the extent that their maps agree on the forms that are exchanged.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: This reframing has a striking consequence.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: It makes *meaning* a property of a *map*, not of a *symbol*.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: A symbol has no intrinsic meaning; it has meaning only relative to the map $\pi$ and the space $S$ into which it is sent.
statements.section: The semantic space $S$ and the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$

statements.quote: This is a topological version of the classic semantic insight that meaning is use, but stated in the language of spaces and maps.

statements.quote: The map $\pi$ sends each form into a space $S$ that has a structure of its own — and that structure mirrors, point for point, the scale-structure of $X$.
statements.section: The hierarchy of semantic structure

statements.quote: Meanings are not a flat set; they are organized in a hierarchy.
statements.section: The hierarchy of semantic structure

statements.quote: At the lowest level are *atomic* meanings — the meanings of simple predicates and objects (DOG, RUN, RED).
statements.section: The hierarchy of semantic structure

statements.quote: Above them are *compositional* meanings, built from atomic ones by the operations of the language ($AGENT(DOG, RUN)$).
statements.section: The hierarchy of semantic structure

statements.quote: Above those are *relational* and *eventual* meanings — situations and scenarios — and above them still, *discourse-level* meanings: narratives, arguments, implications.
statements.section: The hierarchy of semantic structure

statements.quote: The key geometric claim is that this hierarchy is not a chain of separate levels but a *nested, self-similar* structure: the same geometric operations (composition, combination, filling-in) that build a compositional meaning from atomic ones also build a discourse meaning from event meanings.
statements.section: The hierarchy of semantic structure

statements.quote: The hierarchy of meaning is, in this view, the same hierarchy of scale that $X$ exhibits.
statements.section: The hierarchy of semantic structure

statements.quote: This is what lets the principle "structures are built from structures" apply to meaning itself: a complex meaning is not a new primitive but a *structure of* simpler meanings.
statements.section: The hierarchy of semantic structure

statements.quote: The semantic space $S$ is therefore a *hierarchical fractal* — a space whose parts are, in a precise sense, smaller copies of the whole.
statements.section: The hierarchy of semantic structure

statements.quote: So far we have two spaces, $X$ and $S$, and a map $\pi: X \to S$.
statements.section: The three-space picture: $X$, $S$, and the world

statements.quote: But $S$, the space of semantic structures, is itself not the final word.
statements.section: The three-space picture: $X$, $S$, and the world

statements.quote: Meanings are not free-floating; they are *about* something.
statements.section: The three-space picture: $X$, $S$, and the world

statements.quote: They refer to states of affairs, situations, and possibilities in the world.
statements.section: The three-space picture: $X$, $S$, and the world

statements.quote: We therefore introduce a third space, $W$, the space of *worlds* or *states of affairs*: the space of all situations that can be described, imagined, or acted upon.
statements.section: The three-space picture: $X$, $S$, and the world

statements.quote: There is a natural map from $S$ to $W$ (or, more precisely, a *satisfaction* or *truth* relation between $S$ and $W$): a semantic structure is *satisfied* by, or *true in*, a world to the extent that the world matches the situation the structure describes.

statements.quote: The three spaces: linguistic forms $X$, the semantic structures $S$ they map to under interpretation, and the worlds $W$ those structures are about.
statements.section: The three-space picture: $X$, $S$, and the world

statements.quote: Everything so far has treated meaning as *structure* — the shape of $X$, the geometry of $S$, the map between them.
statements.section: Semantics as structure, not label

statements.quote: It is time to say plainly what this view excludes.
statements.section: Semantics as structure, not label

statements.quote: The most important conceptual shift in this chapter is a single one: a meaning is not a *label* attached to a point of $X$.
statements.section: Semantics as structure, not label

statements.quote: A label is a name we paste on a configuration — "this point means *DOG-CHASES-CAT*." The geometric view replaces labels with *structure*: a meaning is the *pattern of relations* that a region of $X$ participates in, and it is that pattern — not any intrinsic property of the point — that constitutes the meaning.
statements.section: Semantics as structure, not label

statements.quote: First, *synonymy and paraphrase* are explained naturally: two different points (two different forms) have the same meaning precisely because they sit in the *same structural position* — the same relations to their neighbourhood, the same place in the web.
statements.section: Semantics as structure, not label

statements.quote: Same structure, same meaning, different label.
statements.section: Semantics as structure, not label

statements.quote: Second, *novel meaning* is explained naturally: a new form is meaningful when it is *absorbed into the existing structure* — when it takes up a structural position in the web, even though no label has ever been attached to it before.
statements.section: Semantics as structure, not label

statements.quote: Productivity is the ability to create new points that fit the existing structure.
statements.section: Semantics as structure, not label

statements.quote: This is the topological version of the classic insight that "meaning is use," or that "the meaning of a word is its role in the language." Stated geometrically, it becomes precise: the role of a form *is* its position in a structured space, and that position is a geometric object.
statements.section: Semantics as structure, not label

statements.quote: The title of the chapter promises a foam, and the promise is now kept.
statements.section: The geometry of the web

statements.quote: When the map $\pi$ spreads the forms of $X$ out over the space of meanings, the result is not a uniform haze but a web: dense clusters where convention piles up, thin filaments of productive structure between them, and wide voids where nothing is ever uttered.
statements.section: The geometry of the web

statements.quote: This part names the three features, and then shows how much they explain.
statements.section: The geometry of the web

statements.quote: We now turn to the geometric features of $X$ (and, derivatively, of $S$).
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: The central claim of this chapter is that a meaningful language space has a characteristic *shape*, and that the shape is best described by three kinds of feature:
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: **Clusters** are regions of $X$ that are densely populated and internally cohesive.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: They correspond to *conventional* or *frequent* linguistic configurations: idioms, collocations, grammatical frames, topic domains.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: A cluster is a place where many utterances are close to one another and where the interpretation map $\pi$ is relatively stable and predictable.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: **Filaments** are thin, elongated regions of moderate density that *connect* clusters.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: They correspond to *productive* patterns: grammatical operations, constructions, and schemas that allow one to move from one conventional region to another by a regular, rule-like transformation.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: A filament is a *bridge* between clusters, and it is the structural basis of *productivity* — the ability to generate and understand novel utterances.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: **Voids** are regions of $X$ that are sparsely or not at all populated.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: They correspond to *ungrammatical*, *infelicitous*, or simply *unused* configurations.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: A void is not merely "missing data"; it is a *meaningful absence*.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: The shape of the voids is as informative as the shape of the clusters, because the voids define the boundaries of the possible.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: Together, clusters, filaments, and voids define the *landscape* of the language space.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: The landscape is not uniform: it is a hierarchy of dense regions connected by thin bridges, set against a background of empty space.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: This is precisely the shape that is observed in other complex, scale-free systems — most famously, the large-scale structure of the universe.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: The importance of this trichotomy is that it gives a *geometric* account of three central linguistic phenomena:
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: - **Convention** is *cluster-ness*: the tendency of frequent usage to form dense, stable regions.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: - **Productivity** is *filament-ness*: the existence of regular, connective structure that allows generalization.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: - **Constraint** (grammaticality, felicity) is *void-ness*: the existence of large, structured regions of the possible that are simply not realized.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: A theory of meaning that captures these three features captures, we argue, the essential *shape* of linguistic structure.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: The picture generalizes in a natural way.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: There is not one landscape but a *stack* of coupled ones: a syntactic landscape, a semantic landscape, a grounding landscape, and an epistemic landscape, each with its own clusters, voids, and boundaries, and each correlated with the others.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: Strong syntax tends to make semantic structure more likely; grounding imposes further constraints on what can be meaningful; and the epistemic layer records where the system is certain and where it is still open.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: Meaning is strong where these layers align, and weak or absent where they diverge.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: A stack of coupled landscapes: each layer has its own clusters, voids, and boundaries, and the layers are correlated with one another.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: Meaning is strong where the layers align.
statements.section: Clusters, filaments, and voids

statements.quote: The trichotomy just laid down is more than a description of the landscape; it becomes explanatory as soon as it is put to work.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: Its first job is metaphor.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: Consider the sentence *time is a river*.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: The concepts **TIME** and **RIVER** normally occupy quite different neighbourhoods of the semantic space: one is abstract and temporal, the other concrete and physical.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: And yet the sentence is immediately, richly meaningful.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: The picture of the previous section suggests an answer.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: A metaphor does not place a new point inside an existing cluster; it **creates a connection between two regions that are not ordinarily adjacent**.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: It weaves a *filament* — a narrow bridge of structure — across the void that separates them.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: **[SPECULATION]** Metaphor is therefore a mechanism that creates or strengthens *long-range* connections between otherwise separated semantic regions.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: This makes it structurally different from ordinary local similarity ("dog" sits near "cat"): local similarity moves *within* a cluster, whereas metaphor opens a *new filament* between clusters.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: Seen through the lens of **homotopy type theory**, this is exactly the right way to think about it.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: In HoTT a *path* between two points is not a bare assertion that they are related — it is a *witness of a transformation* that carries one to the other.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: A metaphorical filament is precisely such a path: it does not merely link TIME and RIVER, it *transports structure* from one region to the other.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: The words *flow, current, depth, bank, source, mouth* are the local data of the path — the specific relations it carries across.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: Two metaphors can connect the same two regions by *different* paths (different mappings), and it is the content of the path that makes one metaphor fruitful and another empty.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: In this sense a metaphor is a **meaningful transformation**: a path whose interior structure is itself semantic content.
statements.section: Metaphor as a filament

statements.quote: The map $\pi$ has carried the whole chapter so far, but only as a single arrow between two spaces.
statements.section: The structure of interpretation

statements.quote: An arrow is too little: $\pi$ has an internal structure — each meaning is covered by a whole family of forms — and it must *respect* the structure of language, which is exactly what a commutative diagram says.
statements.section: The structure of interpretation

statements.quote: This part examines the map itself, and then follows it all the way to the world, where a truth condition anchors meaning to fact.
statements.section: The structure of interpretation

statements.quote: The map $\pi: X \to S$ invites a more sophisticated geometric treatment.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: If we view $\pi$ as a **fiber bundle** projection, then each point $s \in S$ (a meaning) has a **fiber** $\pi^{-1}(s) \subseteq X$ over it: the set of all linguistic forms that express that meaning.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: The fiber-bundle view has several consequences:
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: **Meanings are the base; forms are the fibers.** The "real" structure is in the base space $S$; the forms in $X$ are the many-to-one covering of that structure.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: Two forms that are far apart in $X$ may lie in the same fiber, and hence express the same meaning.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: **Paraphrase is a path within a fiber.** To paraphrase is to move from one point in a fiber to another, staying over the same meaning.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: The geometry of a fiber is the geometry of *paraphrase*: the space of all ways of saying the same thing.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: **Synonymy is a property of fibers, not of points.** Two words are synonyms not in an absolute sense, but relative to a meaning: they are close in $X$ *within the same fiber*.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: Synonymy is a fiber-local relation.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: **The bundle can have non-trivial topology — and paths act on fibers.** The fibers need not be trivial products; the bundle over $S$ can have *twists* and *monodromy*.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: In the language of homotopy type theory each fiber is a *type* sitting over its base point, and a *path* in the base $S$ *transports* a point of one fiber to a point of another — the action of a path, also called *monodromy*.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: Travel once around a loop in $S$ and a form can be carried back to a *different* form in the same fiber.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: This is the precise sense in which "the way of saying" a meaning can depend on the *path* by which one arrives at it: meaning is path-dependent, exactly as identity types are in a type theory.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: The fiber-bundle picture is, we think, the right level of mathematical abstraction for the relation between form and meaning.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: It captures the many-to-one nature of interpretation, the locality of paraphrase and synonymy, and the global complexity of the form–meaning relation.
statements.section: The fiber-bundle view: meaning as a family of structures

statements.quote: We can now state the central structural claim of the theory as a *commutativity* condition.

statements.quote: The three spaces $X$, $S$, and $W$, together with the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$ and the satisfaction relation between $S$ and $W$, should be organized so that the different routes from a form to a world *agree*.

statements.quote: What stitches that seam to the world is truth — and the canonical statement of this bond remains Tarski's.

statements.quote: Tarski's semantic conception of truth begins with the sentence "Snow is white" and points out the difference between the *expression* and the *state of affairs* it expresses.

statements.quote: In the geometric view, that difference becomes a map.
statements.section: Tarski and the world: where meaning meets fact

statements.quote: The linguistic expression "Snow is white" lives in the linguistic space $X$.

statements.quote: Its meaning — the proposition that snow is white — lives in the semantic space $S$.
statements.section: Tarski and the world: where meaning meets fact

statements.quote: And the *fact* that makes it true (the state of affairs that snow is white) lives in the world space $W$.
statements.section: Tarski and the world: where meaning meets fact

statements.quote: and the final step is a *truth*: the world condition is satisfied in some world $w \in W$.

statements.quote: In model-theoretic terms, the interpretation assigns to each sentence $s$ the set of worlds in which it is true:
statements.section: Tarski and the world: where meaning meets fact

statements.quote: Meaning is, in Tarski's sense, *about the world*: it is the set of possible worlds in which the sentence holds.

statements.quote: Two sentences with the same truth conditions have the same meaning.
statements.section: Tarski and the world: where meaning meets fact

statements.quote: This is exactly the fiber-bundle picture: all the linguistic forms that are true in precisely the same set of worlds lie in the same fiber over $S$.
statements.section: Tarski and the world: where meaning meets fact

statements.quote: The three-space picture ($X \to S \leftrightarrow W$) thus has a sharp, testable reading: the semantic space $S$ is not a free-floating abstract object, but is *tethered to the world* by the truth-conditions of its points.

statements.quote: A theory of shapes is only as good as its ability to measure them, and nothing so far has said how the shape of a language space could be detected in data.
statements.section: Measuring the shape

statements.quote: The instruments come from topology: invariants that survive a change of coordinates or a change of scale.
statements.section: Measuring the shape

statements.quote: This part introduces them, shows concretely how they are computed on a point cloud, and draws the line between the instrument and the theory it serves.
statements.section: Measuring the shape

statements.quote: If the shape of $X$ is the object of study, then the right tools are *topological invariants*: quantities that capture the shape of a space without depending on a particular embedding or coordinate system.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: The most important of these, for our purposes, are:
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: **Connected components.** The zeroth-level structure: how many separate "islands" of language are there, and how are they connected?
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: A language with many disconnected components is one in which some regions of meaning are simply unreachable from others.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: **Holes (higher homotopy / homology groups).** The presence of non-trivial loops and voids in $X$.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: A "hole" in the language space is a region that is surrounded by language but not itself filled — a *systematic gap*.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: The topology of the holes is a measure of the *complexity* of the space: how many independent ways can one go "around" a void?
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: **Persistent homology.** Because $X$ is multi-scale, the right invariant is not a single set of homology groups but a *family* of them, indexed by scale.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: Persistent homology tracks which topological features (components, loops, voids) appear at one scale and persist or disappear at another.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: This is exactly the tool needed to study a scale-free, self-similar space, and it is already a mature method in topological data analysis.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: The claim of this section is that the **topological invariants of $X$ are the "shape of meaning"**.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: Two language spaces with the same topological invariants have the same *shape*, even if their metrics, measures, and embeddings differ.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: Meaning, in this view, is *topological*: it is a property of the shape of the space, invariant under continuous deformation.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: This is a strong and checkable claim.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: It says that the meaningful content of a language is not in the particular words or the particular frequencies, but in the *persistent shape* of the space of possible utterances.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: It is the claim that two very different languages (or two very different models of the same language) that have the same persistent homology are, in the deep structural sense, *the same language*.
statements.section: Topological invariants and the "shape" of meaning

statements.quote: Concretely, suppose a discourse is represented by points $P_T = \{x_1,\dots,x_k\}$ in a high-dimensional representation space.

statements.quote: Temporarily ignoring order, one builds the **Vietoris–Rips filtration** $VR(P_T,\epsilon)$: two points are joined by an edge whenever their distance is at most $\epsilon$, and a triangle is filled in whenever all three of its edges are present.
statements.section: How one measures the shape: the Vietoris–Rips filtration

statements.quote: As $\epsilon$ grows from zero, points connect, components merge, loops appear, and holes fill in.
statements.section: How one measures the shape: the Vietoris–Rips filtration

statements.quote: Persistent homology records, for each topological feature, the $\epsilon$ at which it is *born* and the $\epsilon$ at which it *dies*.
statements.section: How one measures the shape: the Vietoris–Rips filtration

statements.quote: The result is not automatically a two-dimensional surface — it is a simplicial complex with potentially high-dimensional topology.
statements.section: How one measures the shape: the Vietoris–Rips filtration

statements.quote: The multiscale "shape signature" of the discourse is the family
statements.section: How one measures the shape: the Vietoris–Rips filtration

statements.quote: the Betti numbers at every scale.
statements.section: How one measures the shape: the Vietoris–Rips filtration

statements.quote: Two configurations can then be compared by a distance between their persistence structures,
statements.section: How one measures the shape: the Vietoris–Rips filtration

statements.quote: and the empirical question becomes: *do semantically related structures have systematically related topological signatures?*
statements.section: How one measures the shape: the Vietoris–Rips filtration

statements.quote: It is worth stressing what persistent homology is — and is not.
statements.section: Topology is a measurement tool, not the theory

statements.quote: It is a possible **measurement tool**, not the theory itself.
statements.section: Topology is a measurement tool, not the theory

statements.quote: The deeper hypothesis is that meaningful language possesses *stable multiscale relational organisation*.
statements.section: Topology is a measurement tool, not the theory

statements.quote: Several complementary perspectives probe the same space from different angles:
statements.section: Topology is a measurement tool, not the theory

statements.quote: - **Topology** asks: *which structures survive a change of scale?*
statements.section: Topology is a measurement tool, not the theory

statements.quote: - **Fractal analysis** asks: *how does structural complexity scale?*
statements.section: Topology is a measurement tool, not the theory

statements.quote: - **Geometry** asks: *how are structures separated and clustered?*
statements.section: Topology is a measurement tool, not the theory

statements.quote: - **Network analysis** asks: *which structures connect to which others?*
statements.section: Topology is a measurement tool, not the theory

statements.quote: - **Information geometry** asks: *how are probability distributions and uncertainties organised?*
statements.section: Topology is a measurement tool, not the theory

statements.quote: None of these is the whole story; together they are the instrument panel of the geometric view.

statements.quote: The structure has been described, but where does it come from?
statements.section: Learning the foam

statements.quote: Neither a child nor a model is handed the map $\pi$; both must build it from samples, and the geometry predicts exactly how such construction has to go.

statements.quote: This part states the prediction twice — once for a general learner, once for a transformer doing nothing but next-token prediction.

statements.quote: We can now give a geometric account of **language learning**.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: To learn a language is to construct, from experience, an approximation to the interpretation map $\pi: X \to S$.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: The learner is presented with pairs $(x, s)$ — forms and their meanings (or, more realistically, forms and situations in $W$ that the form is used in) — and must infer the map $\pi$ that sends forms to meanings.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: This is a *function-learning* problem, but with a crucial geometric structure: the map $\pi$ is not arbitrary.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: It is constrained by the geometry of $X$ (the learner can only learn from the regions of $X$ that are actually encountered) and by the commutativity condition (the map must preserve structure).
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: The geometric view explains several well-known facts about learning:
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: - **The poverty of the stimulus** is a *coverage* problem: the learner only sees a small, biased sample of $X$, concentrated in the high-frequency clusters.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: Learning requires *generalizing* from the clusters to the filaments and the (unseen) structure of the tail.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: - **Productivity in acquisition** — the child's ability to produce and understand novel sentences — is the emergence of *filaments*: the learner has inferred the connective structure that links clusters, not merely memorized the clusters themselves.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: - **The "critical period"** may be a *topological* phenomenon: early in development, the geometry of $X$ is still being laid down, and the topology is plastic; later, the topology becomes fixed, and only local (metric) adjustments are possible.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: The geometry also predicts *how* generalization works, and here the theory meets a classic result from cognition.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: Shepard proposed a **universal law of generalization**: the probability that a response learned to one stimulus transfers to another is an exponentially decreasing function of the distance between the two stimuli in a *psychological space* \cite{shepard1987universal}.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: where $d(x,x')$ is the distance in the representational space.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: The bold claim is that this form is *universal* — across species, tasks, and modalities — because it is the form any internalized, distance-based decision rule must take.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: In the language of this chapter, the law says **generalization is local in $X$**: the closer an unseen form is to a known one, the more reliably its meaning transfers, and the more distant it is, the less.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: Shepard's exponential kernel is precisely what turns the metric of $X$ into a *learning* signal — and one of the clearest pieces of evidence that the right language for meaning is the language of spaces and distances.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: The upshot is that learning is not the accumulation of facts but the *construction of a map between spaces*, under geometric constraints.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: This reframes the central problem of language acquisition as a problem in *topological inference*: inferring the shape of a space and the structure of a map from partial, noisy observations.
statements.section: Learning as the construction of $\pi$

statements.quote: It is shown a corpus and asked to predict the next token, and from that single repeated error it must do something harder than memorize: it must locate the web.

statements.quote: Its one way to reduce its loss is to discover where the corpus actually lives — the clusters, and above all the **filaments** that connect them — and to learn to walk only there.

statements.quote: **[HYPOTHESIS]** A fully trained model assigns probability concentrated on the web, and exponentially small probability in the voids; the interesting part is directional.

statements.quote: $\pi_\theta$ is, in effect, a vector field on $X$ whose integral curves follow the filaments: sampling is a random walk that stays on the web, threading clusters, crossing filaments, and only rarely venturing into a void.

statements.quote: What has been assembled here is a scaffold, not a building, and a scaffold is only useful if it points at work to be done.
statements.section: The research programme

statements.quote: This part turns the chapter into an agenda: the open problems the theory must solve, the four-level programme that would solve them, the results that would count as evidence, and the methodological risks that must be kept in view while the work proceeds.
statements.section: The research programme

statements.quote: The open problems are the places where the scaffold needs to be turned into a building.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: We close with the most important of them.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: **Problem 1 (Existence and construction of $X$).** We have described $X$ as the space of all potential linguistic configurations, but we have not *constructed* it.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: What is the precise topological space?
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: A metric space, a simplicial complex, a topos?
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: The answer will determine which invariants are available.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: **Problem 2 (The interpretation map $\pi$).** We have treated $\pi$ as a given.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: But $\pi$ is not observed directly; it is inferred.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: What are the precise constraints that determine $\pi$?
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: Is it a morphism in a specific category?
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: The commutativity condition is a start, but it is not a full specification.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: **Problem 3 (The heavy tail and meaning).** We have claimed that meaning lives in the heavy tail.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: This needs to be made precise and tested.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: What is the measurable signature of "meaning in the tail"?
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: Can it be detected in persistent homology, in the geometry of the tail, or in the behavior of $\pi$ on low-frequency forms?
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: **Problem 4 (Self-similarity and scale).** The claim that $X$ is approximately self-similar needs a precise formulation.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: Is there a genuine scaling symmetry, or only statistical scale-invariance?
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: What are the exponents, and do they vary across languages?
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: **Problem 5 (The three spaces and truth).** The space $W$ of worlds, and the satisfaction relation $S \models W$, are the least developed parts of the picture.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: How does the geometry of $W$ interact with the geometry of $S$?
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: This is where the theory must connect to formal semantics and to the philosophy of truth.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: These five problems are not independent.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: They form a programme: construct the spaces, specify the maps, identify the invariants, test the heavy-tail claim, and connect the geometry to truth.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: A theory of meaningful language spaces is complete when it can answer all five.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: The aim of this chapter has not been to answer these questions, but to make them *visible*.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: The hope is that the geometric and topological language gives a shared vocabulary in which the right questions can be asked, and in which progress can be measured.
statements.section: Open problems and a research programme

statements.quote: The five problems are best read as a four-level programme, each level providing the infrastructure for the next:
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: - **Level 1 — Formal foundations.** Construct the space $X$ and the semantic space $S$; define the interpretation map $\pi$ and the satisfaction relation $S \models W$; and fix the class of structure-preserving maps.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: *Deliverables:* a precise definition of the three spaces; a specification of $\pi$; a proof that the diagram commutes.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: - **Level 2 — Topological and geometric invariants.** Identify the invariants (connected components, holes, persistent homology, fractal dimension, clustering statistics) that should be preserved by $\pi$ and by the structure-preserving maps.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: *Deliverables:* a catalogue of invariants; a proof that they are well-defined on $X$ and $S$; a comparison of the invariant signatures of two related structures.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: - **Level 3 — Empirical testing.** Represent real linguistic data as points in $X$, compute the invariants, and test the predictions.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: *Deliverables:* a benchmark of invariant signatures across corpora and languages; a demonstration that semantically related structures have closer invariant signatures; a demonstration that the heavy tail carries persistent structure.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: - **Level 4 — Integration and unification.** Show that the invariants of $X$, $S$, and $W$ fit together into a single coherent picture, and that the theory *explains* — not merely describes — compositionality, ambiguity, metaphor, and learning.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: *Deliverables:* a unified account; a set of novel, testable predictions; a bridge to formal semantics and to the cognitive science of meaning.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: The levels are cumulative.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: Nothing at Level 3 is meaningful without the invariants of Level 2, and nothing at Level 2 without the spaces of Level 1.
statements.section: The research programme: four levels

statements.quote: The programme is complete when Level 4 produces a unified, predictive, and testable account of meaning.

statements.quote: A research programme must be *falsifiable*, and the geometric view makes that explicit.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: The most important empirical predictions, in increasing order of ambition, are:
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: **Persistent topology.** The persistent-homology signature of a meaningful corpus is stable across paraphrase, translation, and register change, while the detailed metric is not.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: **Topological similarity.** Semantically related structures (same meaning, different form) have topologically similar signatures; unrelated structures do not.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: **Heavy-tail structure.** The low-frequency tail carries *persistent* topological structure (not merely noise), systematically related to the high-frequency core.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: **Compositional commutativity.** The interpretation map approximately commutes with composition — the meaning of a composition is close to the composition of the meanings — and the failure to commute is small and structured.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: **Scale-free invariants.** The topological and clustering invariants are approximately scale-free, with exponents that are stable across languages (universality) rather than language-specific.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: **Metaphor as structure.** Productive metaphors map a *structured* source region onto a *structured* target region and preserve the relevant invariants; dead metaphors and random word-pairings do not.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: **Learning as topological inference.** Language learning is best described as the progressive construction of the topology of $X$ — clusters first, then filaments, then the large-scale shape.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: **Universality classes.** Distantly related or unrelated languages that share a domain of meaning fall into the same universality class: the same large-scale invariants, different micro-structure.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: **The world-anchor.** The satisfaction relation $S \models W$ is itself structured: worlds that are close in a natural geometry satisfy similar sets of semantic structures, and this geometry is detectable.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: Each of these is, in principle, checkable with existing methods — persistent homology, clustering, scaling analysis.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: None has yet been checked in this way.
statements.section: What would count as evidence

statements.quote: That is the work the programme describes.

statements.quote: To remain honest, the framework must confront its own methodological risks:
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: - **The risk of emptiness.** A theory stated in the language of "spaces" and "maps" can always be made true by choosing the right spaces and the right maps.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: The defence is the research programme: the spaces must be *constructed*, the maps *specified*, and the invariants *computed on real data*.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: A framework that cannot produce a number is a metaphor, not a theory.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: - **The risk of circularity.** Defining meaning by reference to meaning (via $\pi$) risks circularity.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: The defence is the world-anchor: the satisfaction relation $S \models W$ ties meaning to the world independently of the linguistic map, and the geometry of $W$ must be specified by something other than $\pi$.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: - **The risk of the map being the territory.** The spaces $X$ and $S$ are *models* of language, not language itself.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: Their worth is measured by the accuracy and scope of their predictions, not by their aesthetic appeal.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: The cosmic-web analogy is a *structural* claim, not an identity claim.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: - **The burden of precision.** Every claim in this chapter is currently at the level of a conjecture with an illustration, not a theorem with a proof.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: The value of the chapter is that it makes the conjectures *precise enough to be checked*; its failure mode is to remain forever at the level of illustration.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: The four-level programme is the answer to that failure mode.
statements.section: A methodological caution

statements.quote: Every section so far has contributed one piece of a single picture; it remains to put the pieces together.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: Put together, the pieces give a single picture.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: There is a space $X$ of all possible linguistic configurations, a space $S$ of semantic structures, and a space $W$ of worlds.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: A map $\pi: X \to S$ (interpretation) and a relation $S \models W$ (truth) connect them in a diagram that commutes.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: The space $X$ is a structured landscape — clusters of common forms, filaments of compositionality, voids of systematic gaps — that is approximately scale-free.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: Meaning is the *structure* of this landscape and of the map $\pi$, not a list of labels attached to points.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: Learning is the construction of $\pi$; metaphor is a path between distant clusters; and the deep content of a language is the *persistent shape* of its space.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: That is the central claim of this chapter, stated as plainly as it can be: **meaning is the geometry and topology of the space of possible utterances, and understanding is the knowledge of that shape.**
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: This chapter develops a geometric and topological view of meaningful language.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: The central ideas — meaning as structure, the three-space picture, and the landscape of clusters, filaments, and voids — draw on several traditions.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **Structural semantics and the relational nature of meaning.** The view that meaning is relational and that a sign's value comes from its differences within a system is classical.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: The model-theoretic treatment of meaning, truth, and satisfaction is due to Tarski, whose definition of truth for formal languages is the direct ancestor of the satisfaction relation $S \models W$ used here.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{tarski1935wahrheitsbegriff}, \citealternativetitle{tarski1935wahrheitsbegriff} (\citeyear{tarski1935wahrheitsbegriff}).
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{hodges1993modeltheory}, \citealternativetitle{hodges1993modeltheory} (\citeyear{hodges1993modeltheory}) — a modern, accessible account of the model theory that underlies the $S$–$W$ relation.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **Metaphor and structural mapping.** The claim that metaphor works by mapping relational structure from a source domain to a target domain is the central result of the cognitive-linguistic programme on metaphor.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{lakoff1993metaphor}, \citealternativetitle{lakoff1993metaphor} (\citeyear{lakoff1993metaphor}) — the standard statement of the conceptual-metaphor thesis.

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{gentner1983structuremapping}, \citealternativetitle{gentner1983structuremapping} (\citeyear{gentner1983structuremapping}) — the structure-mapping theory that motivates the "common structural skeleton" condition on fruitful metaphors.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **Topological data analysis and the shape of data.** The use of topological invariants — connected components, holes, and above all persistent homology — to extract the "shape" of a high-dimensional data set is the methodological core of the geometric view.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{edelsbrunner2002persistent}, \citealternativetitle{edelsbrunner2002persistent} (\citeyear{edelsbrunner2002persistent}) — the founding paper on persistent homology.

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{carlsson2009tda}, \citealternativetitle{carlsson2009tda} (\citeyear{carlsson2009tda}) — the survey that introduced topological data analysis to a broad audience.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **Algebraic topology.** The background definitions of topological spaces, homotopy, homology, and fiber bundles used throughout the chapter are standard.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{hatcher}, \citealternativetitle{hatcher} (\citeyear{hatcher}) — the standard reference for algebraic topology.

statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **The cosmic web as a model landscape.** The picture of a space organized into clusters, filaments, and voids is borrowed directly from the observed large-scale structure of the universe.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{cosmic_web_image}, \citealternativetitle{cosmic_web_image} (\citeyear{cosmic_web_image}) — the cosmic-web visualization used as the model for the landscape of a language space.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **Scale-free structure and heavy tails in language.** The empirical facts about Zipf's law and heavy-tailed distributions in language are well documented.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{zipf1949human}, \citealternativetitle{zipf1949human} (\citeyear{zipf1949human}) — the book that popularised Zipf's law (the rank–frequency regularity had been noted earlier, by Estoup in 1916 and Condon in 1928).
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{statisticsofextremes}, \citealternativetitle{statisticsofextremes} — on the statistics of heavy-tailed phenomena.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **Generalization and psychological space.** The claim that generalization falls off with distance in a representational space is the classic "universal law of generalization."
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{shepard1987universal}, \citealternativetitle{shepard1987universal} (\citeyear{shepard1987universal}) — the original statement: the probability of generalizing a response decays exponentially with distance in a psychological space.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **Conceptual spaces and the geometry of thought.** The picture of meaning as geometry in quality spaces — objects as points, properties as regions, similarity as distance, and natural properties as convex regions (criterion P) — is the cognitive-science ancestor of the Voronoi picture this chapter builds.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{gardenfors2000conceptual}, \citealternativetitle{gardenfors2000conceptual} (\citeyear{gardenfors2000conceptual}) — quality spaces, the three levels of cognitive resolution, prototypes whose convex Voronoi regions fall out of nearest-seed assignment (lemma 3.1), and the convexity of natural properties (criterion P), with colour terms as the worked example.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **The Voronoi picture and the geometry of decoding.** The claim that a transformer's hidden states live on a latent semantic manifold and that tokens are its Voronoi regions — with a measured margin, a linearly growing expressibility gap, and a size-independent "hard core" of ambiguity — is the formal, machine side of the same geometry.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{mabrok2026latent}, \citealternativetitle{mabrok2026latent} (\citeyear{mabrok2026latent}) — the latent semantic manifold, the Voronoi margin and expressibility gap, the coarea-based linear scaling of the gap, the rate-distortion bound on finite vocabularies, and the intrinsic-dimension hourglass.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: **The geometry of not-enough-data.** The victory of overparameterized models is often treated as a mystery; the manifold hypothesis resolves it, with a theorem identifying exactly where training can and cannot write.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{he2023sideeffects}, \citealternativetitle{he2023sideeffects} (\citeyear{he2023sideeffects}) — proves that a network trained on low-dimensional data is pinned down on the data manifold while its variation in the normal (void) directions is fixed by initialization alone; the sample-count price of regularizing the voids ($N \sim \sigma^{-2}$) and the slow-convergence price of doing so.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: - \citeauthor{jablonka2025geometry}, \citealternativetitle{jablonka2025geometry} (\citeyear{jablonka2025geometry}) — an accessible statement of the same geometry: learning is the fitting of smooth functions to low-dimensional structure, and every failure mode (shift, adversarial perturbation, extrapolation) is a query that leaves the manifold.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: The chapter is a synthesis of these traditions into a single geometric framework.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: It is a proposal, not a consensus; the open problems in the final section are where the framework meets its tests.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: The analogy between the large-scale structure of the universe and the structure of a language space is sometimes dismissed as mere decoration.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: It is worth saying why it is not.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: The cosmic web is not just *similar in appearance* to the landscape we have described; it is *the same mathematical object*.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: Both are high-dimensional spaces with a measure (mass density, or utterance frequency) that is concentrated in clusters, connected by filaments, and separated by voids.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: Both are believed to be approximately scale-free.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: And both are studied with the same tools: statistics of the density field, and increasingly, topological data analysis.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: The difference is only in the *physics* that generates the structure: gravity and dark matter in the universe; grammar, convention, and use in language.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: The *geometry* is shared.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: That is what makes the analogy a genuine structural one, and what makes the cosmologist's toolkit — clustering statistics, filament detection, void analysis, persistent homology — directly transferable to the study of language.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: The claim is not that language *is* a universe.
statements.section: The central picture

statements.quote: It is that language, like the universe, is a *structured distribution in a high-dimensional space*, and that the mathematics of such distributions is the same in both cases.
statements.section: The central picture
